slides.text:
A command has one main function, `Run`. **Hooks** are extra functions cobra calls around it, so setup and cleanup live apart from the command's own work.

The snippet is pseudo code.
slides.code:
hook runs
the command runs
hook runs

slides.text:
Three sessions:

- **Session 1:** the plain and persistent hooks around `Run`
- **Session 2:** hooks on subcommands: what they inherit and what they replace
- **Session 3:** hooks that fail, and setup for every command

A command has two pairs of hooks: `PreRun` and `PostRun`, and the persistent `PersistentPreRun` and `PersistentPostRun`. Each is a field of the command and a function with the same signature as `Run`.
Cobra calls every hook at a fixed point of the run. To see the order, the hooks in these exercises print a line, so the output is the order.

The persistent hooks sit outside the plain ones. Subcommands will inherit them.
chunks.text:
root := &cobra.Command{
        Use:               "app",
        PersistentPreRun:  say("persistent pre"),
        PreRun:            say("pre"),
        Run:               say("run"),
        PostRun:           say("post"),
        PersistentPostRun: say("persistent post"),
    }

run
post

exercises.title: Which order?
exercises.guide: `say` prints its text on its own line. Pick the order the lines come out.
exercises.code:
root := &cobra.Command{
    Use:               "app",
    PersistentPostRun: say("a"),
    PostRun:           say("b"),
    Run:               say("c"),
    PreRun:            say("d"),
    PersistentPreRun:  say("e"),
}
root.Execute()
exercises.explanation: The order is fixed by cobra: persistent pre, pre, Run, post, persistent post. Where the fields sit in the struct changes nothing.

slides.text:
Commands form a tree. A **persistent** hook belongs to its command and to every subcommand below it. A plain hook belongs only to the command that declares it.

The snippet is pseudo code.
slides.code:
root    persistent hook
  build    Run
  test     Run

slides.text: When two levels of the tree both define the same hook, one of them wins. The exercises show which one, and how to keep both.

slides.text:
Every hook has an `E` version that returns an `error`: `PreRunE`, `PostRunE` and the persistent ones. Cobra reports that error the way it does for `RunE`.

Flags are parsed before any hook runs, so a hook can already read them.
Outside the tree, `cobra.OnInitialize` registers functions for the whole program, and `cobra.OnFinalize` registers the ones that run at the very end. Both are calls, not fields.

exercises.explanation: The post hooks run only after `Run` succeeds. When `RunE` returns an error, they are skipped, so cleanup placed there does not happen on failure.

exercises.title: Hooks and --help
exercises.guide: The user runs `app --help`. What happens to the hooks?
exercises.code:
root := &cobra.Command{
    Use:              "app",
    PersistentPreRun: say("setup"),
    PreRun:           say("check"),
    Run:              say("running"),
}
root.Execute()
options: Setup, check and running, then the help
Only the help text: no hook and no Run
Check and running, then the help text
exercises.explanation: Cobra sees the help flag before it calls any hook, prints the help and stops. Neither the hooks nor `Run` are reached.
